title: 26 U.S. Code Section 41(b)(1) Qualified Research Expenses
description: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1), qualified research expenses are limited to in-house and contract research expenses paid in carrying on a trade or business.

body.text: Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1), qualified research expenses (QREs) are limited to in-house research expenses and contract research expenses that a taxpayer pays or incurs in carrying on a trade or business. This applies to U.S. businesses claiming the federal R&D tax credit, and only expenses expressly listed in § 41(b) qualify; Georgia's state credit adopts this same definition.

Under 26 U.S. Code (U.S.C.) § 41(b)(1), "qualified research expenses" (QREs) are statutorily defined as the sum of two exclusive expenditure categories paid or incurred by a taxpayer during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer: (A) in-house research expenses and (B) contract research expenses. This foundational federal provision restricts the Research and Development (R&D) tax credit to direct, quantifiable outlays for internal employee wages, non-depreciable tangible supplies, qualifying computer time-sharing, and risk-bearing third-party research contracts, systematically excluding general and administrative (G&A) overhead, capital equipment, and routine production costs. When this federal baseline is incorporated into the State of Georgia's Research Tax Credit under Official Code of Georgia Annotated (O.C.G.A.) § 48-7-40.12 and Georgia Department of Revenue (DoR) Rule 560-7-8-.42, taxpayers must satisfy both the federal statutory standards of Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41 and stringent state-level requirements—including a mandatory federal credit prerequisite, strict industry-sector gatekeeping, an absolute in-state geographic nexus, a gross-receipts-indexed base amount formula, and a shortened five-year carryforward window for credits generated in taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025.
Part I: Statutory Deconstruction of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1) Qualified Research Expenses
Legislative Evolution and the Incremental Credit Architecture

The federal Credit for Increasing Research Activities—commonly referred to as the R&D tax credit—is a non-refundable general business credit under IRC § 38 originally enacted by the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (ERTA 1981) as IRC § 44F to incentivize domestic research investment. Subsequent statutory revisions redesignated the credit as IRC § 30 under the Tax Reform Act of 1984 and as IRC § 41 under the Tax Reform Act of 1986, before the Protecting Americans from Tax Hikes (PATH) Act of 2015 made the credit a permanent fixture of the Internal Revenue Code. Under current law in force (26 U.S.C. § 41(a)(1)), a taxpayer's regular research credit equals 20 percent of the excess (if any) of the taxpayer's qualified research expenses for the taxable year over the statutory base amount, plus 20 percent of basic research payments determined under § 41(e)(1)(A) and 20 percent of amounts paid or incurred in carrying on a trade or business to an energy research consortium for energy research under § 41(a)(3). Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(1)–(3), the regular credit base amount is the product of the taxpayer's fixed-base percentage (capped at a maximum of 16 percent under § 41(c)(3)(C) and rounded to the nearest 1/100th of 1 percent under § 41(c)(3)(D)) and the average annual gross receipts of the taxpayer for the four preceding taxable years, subject to the statutory floor of § 41(c)(2) providing that in no event shall the base amount be less than 50 percent of the qualified research expenses for the credit year. Alternatively, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)(A) (formerly codified at § 41(c)(5)(A)), a taxpayer may elect the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC), equal to 14 percent of so much of the current-year QREs as exceeds 50 percent of the average QREs for the three preceding taxable years (or 6 percent of current-year QREs if the taxpayer had no QREs in any one of the three preceding taxable years under § 41(c)(4)(B)).

In every computational pathway under IRC § 41(a)(1) and § 41(c)(4), the threshold legal determination is whether an expenditure qualifies as a QRE under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1), which restricts QREs to the sum of (A) in-house research expenses and (B) contract research expenses paid or incurred by the taxpayer during the taxable year in carrying on any trade or business of the taxpayer. As the IRS Audit Techniques Guide (ATG) for the Credit for Increasing Research Activities emphasizes, the list of qualifying expenditures in IRC § 41(b) is exclusive; if an expenditure is not expressly enumerated in IRC § 41(b), a taxpayer may not claim it as a QRE.
The "In Carrying On a Trade or Business" Requirement and Startup Exception

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1) and Treasury Regulation (26 CFR) § 1.41-2(a)(1), an in-house research expense or a contract research expense is a QRE only if it is paid or incurred by the taxpayer "in carrying on a trade or business of the taxpayer" at the time the expense is paid or incurred. Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(a)(1) establishes that the phrase "in carrying on a trade or business" has the exact same restrictive legal meaning for IRC § 41(b)(1) as it does for ordinary and necessary business deductions under IRC § 162.

This creates a critical statutory distinction between IRC § 41(b)(1) and research deductions under IRC § 174 (and IRC § 174A, enacted by Public Law 119-21 for domestic research and experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024). Under IRC § 174(a) and 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), expenditures qualify if they are incurred merely "in connection with" a taxpayer's trade or business, which permits deductions for pre-operating research incurred prior to active commercialization. By contrast, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(1) dictates that expenses paid or incurred prior to commencing a new business—as distinguished from expanding an existing trade or business—are not paid or incurred "in carrying on" a trade or business, and therefore fail the general rule of § 41(b)(1). Similarly, under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(1), a contract research expense is disqualified as a QRE if the product or result of the research is intended to be transferred to another party in return for license or royalty payments and the taxpayer does not use the product of the research in the taxpayer's own trade or business.

Under IRC § 41(b)(4), in the case of in-house research expenses (but not contract research expenses), a startup venture is treated as satisfying the trade or business requirement of § 41(b)(1) if, at the time such in-house research expenses are paid or incurred, the principal purpose of the taxpayer in making the expenditures is to use the results of the research in the active conduct of a future trade or business of (A) the taxpayer, or (B) one or more other persons who with the taxpayer are treated as a single taxpayer under the controlled-group aggregation rules of IRC § 41(f)(1).
In-House Research Expenses (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2))

Defined under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A), in-house research expenses constitute the primary driver of corporate QRE claims and are statutorily confined to three exclusive subcategories: (i) employee wages for qualified services, (ii) supplies used in the conduct of qualified research, and (iii) qualifying payments for the right to use computers in the conduct of qualified research.

cells: Wages for Qualified Services

Taxable remuneration subject to withholding under IRC § 3401(a) (W-2 wages, salaries, bonuses, and taxable stock option spreads upon exercise) paid for engaging in, directly supervising, or directly supporting qualified research; includes self-employed earned income under IRC § 401(c)(2).

Excludes non-taxable fringe benefits, 401(k) contributions and employer matching, employer payroll taxes, wages used for the IRC § 51(a) Work Opportunity Credit, and time spent on G&A, sales, or routine production.
Supplies Used in Qualified Research

Tangible property acquired and used in the performance of qualified services by an employee (including materials for non-depreciable "pilot models" and proven "extraordinary utilities" required by the special character of the research).

Strictly excludes land, improvements to land, property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation, intangible costs (licenses, royalties, leases), travel/meals, telephone expenses, standard building utilities, and indirect overhead allocated to self-constructed supplies.
Right to Use Computers (Time-Sharing)

Amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use (time-sharing) computers in the conduct of qualified research (e.g., off-premises cloud compute clusters used for code compilation or simulation).

Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4), the computer must be (1) owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer, (2) located off the taxpayer's premises, and (3) not primarily used by the taxpayer. Disqualified under § 41(b)(2)(A) to the extent the taxpayer receives/accrues compensation from another person for the right to use substantially identical personal property.

body.text: 1. The Tripartite Framework of Qualified Wage Services and the 80% "Substantially All" Rule

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(i), the term "wages" has the meaning assigned by 26 U.S.C. § 3401(a)—all taxable remuneration for services performed by an employee for an employer subject to federal income tax withholding, including base salaries, performance bonuses, and the taxable spread of exercised employee stock options. Referencing Apple Computer, Inc. v. Commissioner and Sun Microsystems v. Commissioner, the IRS ATG specifies that exercised stock option spreads are evaluated for qualified service eligibility by looking to the employee's duties in the grant year, and if the work performed in the grant year qualifies, the taxable spread is included in the QRE computation in the year the option is exercised. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(D)(ii)–(iii), eligible wages also encompass net earned income of self-employed individuals and owner-employees under IRC § 401(c)(1)–(2), but exclude any wages taken into account in determining the Work Opportunity Credit under IRC § 51(a). Contributions to deferred compensation plans such as an IRC § 401(k) arrangement, employer matching contributions, employer payroll taxes, and non-taxable fringe benefits are excluded from § 3401(a) withholding and therefore cannot be claimed as QREs.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1)–(3), employee wages constitute in-house QREs only to the extent paid or incurred for "qualified services," which the statute and regulations divide into three distinct tiers:

items: Engaging in Qualified Research (26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(1)): The actual, hands-on conduct of qualified research—such as a laboratory scientist conducting chemical experiments, a software engineer writing experimental algorithms, or an aerospace engineer executing structural simulations.

Direct Supervision of Qualified Research (26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(2)): The immediate, first-line management of qualified research—such as a lead research scientist or engineering manager directly supervising laboratory experiments or technical development sprints. Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(2) and the IRS ATG explicitly exclude supervision by higher-level managers or corporate officers to whom first-line managers report, even if those higher-level executives are credentialed scientists or engineers, except to the extent those executives personally perform hands-on qualified research or immediate first-line technical supervision as part of their work.

Direct Support of Qualified Research (26 CFR § 1.41-2(c)(3)): Services that directly support persons engaging in the actual conduct or direct supervision of qualified research. Treasury Regulation § 1.41-2(c)(3) enumerates four specific qualifying examples: a secretary typing reports describing laboratory results; a laboratory worker cleaning equipment used in qualified research; a clerk compiling research data; and a machinist machining a part for an experimental model. Conversely, § 1.41-2(c)(3) explicitly disqualifies general and administrative (G&A) or indirect services—such as payroll personnel preparing salary checks for research scientists, an accountant accounting for research expenses, a janitor performing general cleaning of a research laboratory, or corporate officers supervising financial or personnel matters (as well as in-house attorneys preparing patent applications or legal documents, which the IRS ATG identifies as non-qualifying wage expenses).

body.text: When an employee performs both qualified and non-qualified services during a taxable year, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) requires the taxpayer to allocate the employee's wages and claim only the amount attributable to qualified services (typically determined by multiplying the employee's total § 3401(a) wages by the ratio of hours spent performing qualified services to total hours worked). However, 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2) establish a major statutory and regulatory safe harbor: if "substantially all" of the services performed by an employee for the taxpayer during the taxable year consist of qualified services, then 100 percent of the employee's services during the taxable year are treated as qualified services.
2. Qualified Supplies, Pilot Models, Extraordinary Utilities, and Self-Constructed Supplies

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(C), the term "supplies" means any tangible property other than (i) land or improvements to land, and (ii) property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(1), supplies qualify as in-house research expenses only if they are used in the performance of qualified services by an employee of the taxpayer (or a person acting in a similar capacity). Neither the statute nor the Treasury Regulations impose a requirement that tangible property be physically destroyed or consumed; rather, the legal test is whether the item is (1) tangible property, (2) used in the conduct of qualified research, and (3) not land, an improvement to land, or property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation under IRC § 167.

The boundary between qualifying non-depreciable supplies and excluded depreciable capital property is a primary focus of IRS examinations. If a taxpayer purchases capital testing machinery (such as a wind tunnel, environmental test chamber, or 3D printer), the acquisition cost is property of a character subject to the allowance for depreciation and is categorically barred from QRE treatment under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii) (even though depreciation allowances on equipment used in research may qualify under IRC § 174, depreciation itself is never a QRE under IRC § 41). Conversely, under the 2014 final amendments to 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4) (T.D. 9680), a "pilot model" is defined as any representation or model of a product—including a fully functional representation or model of the product or, to the extent § 1.174-2(a)(5) applies, a component of the product—produced to evaluate and resolve uncertainty concerning the product during its development or improvement. Non-depreciable tangible materials (such as titanium, composite resins, electronic sensors, or biological feed and test subjects) used to construct or raise a pilot model qualify as supply QREs, whereas pre-sold commercial production units or prototypes of a character subject to depreciation in the taxpayer's hands are excluded.

General administrative expenses, travel, meals, entertainment, relocation costs, professional dues, royalty or license expenses, and researcher telephone expenses are likewise disqualified as supply QREs. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(i), amounts paid or incurred for general utilities—such as water, electricity, and natural gas used in a building where qualified research is performed—are treated as non-qualifying G&A expenses. However, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(2)(ii) establishes a narrow exception for "extraordinary expenditures" for utilities: to the extent the taxpayer can establish that the special character of the qualified research required additional extraordinary utility expenditures (for example, the incremental high-energy electrical consumption required to operate laser or nuclear research equipment, as distinguished from general laboratory lighting), those additional amounts are treated as qualifying supply QREs. The IRS ATG cautions that merely comparing square-footage electricity usage between an administrative building and a research facility is insufficient to substantiate extraordinary utilities. Moreover, when a taxpayer internally manufactures or fabricates tangible supplies for use in its own research, the IRS Coordinated Issue Paper on Self-Constructed Assets (and the IRS ATG) strictly prohibits rolling indirect costs—specifically depreciation expenses on the taxpayer's manufacturing facilities, general and administrative (G&A) expenses, employee benefit expenses, travel and entertainment expenses, and general overhead—into the cost of self-constructed supplies claimed under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). Under Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) 8.7.1.4, both "extraordinary utilities" and the "allocation of indirect costs to self-constructed supplies" are designated as Appeals Coordinated Issues requiring referral to Technical Guidance as well as formal review and concurrence.
3. Computer Time-Sharing Expenses (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) & 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4))

For taxable years beginning after December 31, 1985, amounts paid or incurred for the lease or rental of personal property are generally excluded from QREs, with one statutory exception: under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(2)(A)(iii) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4), amounts paid or incurred to another person for the right to use (time-sharing) computers in the conduct of qualified research qualify as in-house research expenses.

items: The computer must be owned and operated by someone other than the taxpayer;
The computer must be located off the taxpayer's premises; and
The taxpayer must not be the primary user of the computer.

body.text: Contract Research Expenses (26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)): Statutory Rates and the Three-Part Payer Test

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(1), "contract research expenses" are defined as 65 percent of any amount paid or incurred by the taxpayer in carrying on a trade or business to any person (other than an employee of the taxpayer) for the performance on behalf of the taxpayer of qualified research or services which, if performed by employees of the taxpayer, would constitute qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B). This 35 percent statutory reduction (the "haircut") reflects Congress's determination that third-party contractor billings embed commercial profit margins, indirect overhead, and G&A costs that would be non-qualifying if incurred in-house.

Congress enacted two higher statutory inclusion rates under IRC § 41(b)(3) to encourage collaborative scientific and energy research. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(C), the 65 percent rate is increased to 75 percent for amounts paid or incurred by the taxpayer to a "qualified research consortium" for qualified research conducted on behalf of the taxpayer and one or more unrelated taxpayers (treating all persons treated as a single employer under IRC § 52(a) or (b) as related taxpayers). A qualified research consortium is defined in IRC § 41(b)(3)(C)(ii) as any organization that (I) is described in IRC § 501(c)(3) or § 501(c)(6) and is exempt from tax under § 501(a), (II) is organized and operated primarily to conduct scientific research, and (III) is not a private foundation. Additionally, under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(D), the 65 percent rate is increased to 100 percent for amounts paid or incurred for qualified research that constitutes "energy research" conducted by an eligible small business (employing an annual average of 500 or fewer employees during either of the two preceding calendar years and not 50 percent or more owned by the taxpayer under IRC § 318), an institution of higher education (as defined in 26 U.S.C. § 3304(f)), or a Federal laboratory (as defined in section 4(6) of the Stevenson-Wydler Technology Innovation Act of 1980, 15 U.S.C. § 3703(6)). Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(4), if any contract research expense paid or incurred during a taxable year is attributable to qualified research to be conducted after the close of that taxable year (prepaid research), the expenditure is treated as paid or incurred only during the subsequent taxable year(s) in which the qualified research is actually performed.
To claim an outsourced payment as a contract research expense, the customer/payer must satisfy the three-part test of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2)(i)–(iii):

items: Prior Agreement (§ 1.41-2(e)(2)(i)): The research must be performed pursuant to an agreement entered into prior to the performance of the qualified research. Nevertheless, written agreements, work orders, and statements of work are essential in practice to substantiate that the agreement preceded performance and allocated risk prior to the work.

Performed "On Behalf Of" the Taxpayer (§ 1.41-2(e)(2)(ii) & (e)(3)): The agreement must provide that the research be performed on behalf of the taxpayer. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(3), qualified research is performed "on behalf of" the taxpayer if the taxpayer has a right to the research results; this right need not be exclusive.

Payer Bears the Financial Risk of Failure (§ 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii)): The agreement must require the taxpayer (the payer) to bear the expense even if the research is not successful. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii), if the payer's payment is contingent on the success of the research, the payment is considered paid for the product or result rather than for the performance of research, and that contingent portion is disqualified as a contract research expense of the payer. For example, under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(5) Example 4, if a taxpayer agrees to reimburse a contractor $200x for actual research expenses plus a $100x bonus payable only if the research succeeds, the contingent $100x is excluded entirely, and the taxpayer's contract research expense is limited to $130x (65% of the unconditional $200x).

body.text: Special Rules for Partnerships and Joint Ventures (26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(4))

When research is conducted through a partnership, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(4)(i) dictates that in-house or contract research expenses paid or incurred by the partnership are evaluated at the partnership level to determine whether they were incurred in carrying on a trade or business of the partnership, without regard to the individual trades or businesses of the partners.

However, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(a)(4)(ii) provides a vital "Special Rule" for certain partnerships and joint ventures (taxable as partnerships) that are not carrying on the trade or business to which the research relates. If all partners or venturers are entitled to make independent use of the results of the research, a portion of the joint venture's research expenditures may be treated as QREs directly by the eligible partners under a three-step mathematical formula:

items: Step 1 (Hypothetical Entity Pool — § 1.41-2(a)(4)(ii)(C)): Determine the total QREs of the partnership or joint venture assuming for this purpose that the partnership or joint venture were carrying on the trade or business to which the research relates.

Step 2 (Disqualified Partner Haircut — § 1.41-2(a)(4)(ii)(D)): Reduce this hypothetical QRE pool by the proportionate share of expenses allocable to any partners or venturers who would not be able to claim the expenses as QREs if they had paid or incurred them directly (for example, an investment banking partner not engaged in an active trade or business that uses the research). A non-qualifying partner's proportionate share is determined using that partner's largest share of partnership items of income or gain (excluding gain allocated under IRC § 704(c)). If a partner's distributive share may vary during the period the venture is in effect, the highest share that the partner may receive over the life of the venture must be subtracted.

Step 3 (Eligible Partner Allocation — § 1.41-2(a)(4)(ii)(E)): Allocate the remaining reduced pool of QREs among the eligible partners or venturers who would have been entitled to claim a credit in their own trade or business in the relative proportions that they share deductions for IRC § 174 expenses for that taxable year.

Part II: The Qualified Research Mandate (The Four-Part Test of 26 U.S.C. § 41(d))

An expenditure that fits within the wage, supply, computer time-sharing, or contract categories of 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1) cannot be claimed as a QRE unless the underlying activity constitutes "qualified research" under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(2). Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(1), the taxpayer must satisfy a conjunctive Four-Part Test applied separately to each discrete business component, and the activity must not fall within any of the eight statutory exclusions of IRC § 41(d)(4).
1. The Section 174 / Section 174A Test (Elimination of Uncertainty)

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(A), the activity must be research with respect to which expenditures may be treated as expenses under IRC § 174 (or as domestic research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174A for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, pursuant to P.L. 119-21). Under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(1), expenditures qualify if they are incurred in connection with the taxpayer's trade or business and represent research and development costs in the experimental or laboratory sense—specifically, activities intended to discover information that would eliminate uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a product. Treasury Regulation § 1.174-2(a)(1) defines uncertainty as existing if the information available to the taxpayer does not establish either (1) the capability or method for developing or improving the product, or (2) the appropriate design of the product. Whether expenditures qualify depends on the nature of the activity to which the expenditures relate, not the nature of the product or the level of technological advancement it represents. Moreover, under 26 U.S.C. § 174(e), research expenditures are eligible only to the extent that the amount thereof is reasonable under the circumstances.
2. The Discovering Technological Information Test

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(i) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)–(4), the research must be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature. Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(4), information is technological in nature if the process of experimentation used to discover such information fundamentally relies on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science. Research in the social sciences, arts, or humanities (including economics, business management, and behavioral sciences) is statutorily excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(G) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(8), and efficiency surveys, management functions or techniques, market research, routine data collection, and routine quality control testing are excluded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(D) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(5).

In final regulations issued on January 3, 2001 (T.D. 8930), the Treasury Department and IRS initially required taxpayers to prove that their research was undertaken to obtain knowledge that "exceeds, expands, or refines the common knowledge of skilled professionals in a particular field of science or engineering". Following widespread taxpayer objections and Notice 2001-19, Treasury issued proposed regulations (REG-112991-01) and subsequent final regulations (T.D. 9104, January 2004), codified at 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii), which explicitly abolished the "exceeds, expands, or refines" discovery requirement and confirmed that there is no standalone "discovery" test separate from the uncertainty standard of § 1.174-2(a)(1). Under current law in force (26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(ii) and (a)(4)), a taxpayer may employ existing technologies and rely on existing principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science to eliminate uncertainty specific to the taxpayer's business component, and need not succeed in developing the business component. Furthermore, under the Patent Safe Harbor of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(3)(iii), the issuance of a utility patent by the Patent and Trademark Office under 35 U.S.C. § 151 (excluding design patents under 35 U.S.C. § 171) serves as conclusive evidence that the taxpayer discovered technological information intended to eliminate uncertainty, though a patent is not a precondition for credit eligibility.
3. The Business Component Test and the Shrinking-Back Rule

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(2)(B), the taxpayer must intend that the discovered technological information be useful in the development of a new or improved "business component" of the taxpayer—defined as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention which is to be (i) held for sale, lease, or license, or (ii) used by the taxpayer in a trade or business of the taxpayer. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(C), any plant process, machinery, or technique for the commercial production of a business component is treated as a separate business component distinct from the product being produced.

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(2)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(1), the Four-Part Test must be applied first at the level of the discrete overall business component. If the overall business component fails to satisfy all four tests (for example, if upgrading a single subsystem of an aircraft, motorcycle engine, or software suite represents less than 80% of the total activities on the entire commercial product), 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2) mandates the "shrinking-back rule" (mirrored for Section 174 in 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(5)): the tests are applied to the most significant subset of elements of the business component (such as the carburetor of a motorcycle engine), and shrinking back continues recursively until either a subset of elements satisfies all requirements of IRC § 41(d)(1) or the most basic element of the product or process is reached and fails the test.
4. The Process of Experimentation Test and the 80% "Substantially All" Threshold

Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(1)(C) and § 41(d)(3)(A), "substantially all" of the research activities with respect to the business component must constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose—specifically, a purpose relating to a new or improved (i) function, (ii) performance, or (iii) reliability or quality of the business component. Under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(3)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), research is strictly disqualified if it relates to style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors.

Treasury Regulation 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(i) defines a process of experimentation as a process designed to evaluate one or more alternatives to achieve a result where the capability or method of achieving that result, or the appropriate design of that result, is uncertain as of the beginning of the taxpayer's research activities. The regulation mandates three core evaluative elements fundamentally relying on the hard sciences, engineering, or computer science:

items: Identification of uncertainty concerning the development or improvement of a business component;
Identification of one or more alternatives intended to eliminate that uncertainty; and
Identification and the conduct of a process of evaluating the alternatives (through, for example, modeling, simulation, or a systematic trial and error methodology).

body.text: Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(6), the "substantially all" requirement of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) is satisfied only if 80 percent or more of a taxpayer's research activities for the business component, measured on a cost or other consistently applied reasonable basis (and determined without regard to the employee-level wage safe harbor of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)), constitute elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose. If this 80 percent activity threshold is met, the remaining 20 percent (or less) of research activities with respect to that business component also qualify, provided they satisfy the Section 174 test of § 41(d)(1)(A) and are not excluded under § 41(d)(4)—such as post-commercial-production activities under § 41(d)(4)(A) and § 1.41-4(c)(2), adaptation of an existing business component to a particular customer's requirement under § 41(d)(4)(B) and § 1.41-4(c)(3), duplication or reverse engineering of an existing business component under § 41(d)(4)(C) and § 1.41-4(c)(4), or non-qualifying internal-use software failing the high threshold of innovation test under § 41(d)(4)(E) and § 1.41-4(c)(6).
Part III: The Georgia State R&D Tax Credit Paradigm (O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12)

While federal law under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1) establishes the baseline definition of QREs, the State of Georgia provides a state-level Research Tax Credit (Tax Credit Code 112) governed by O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12 and administered by the Georgia Department of Revenue under Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 560-7-8-.42. Georgia explicitly adopts the federal IRC § 41 definition of QREs, but superimposes five structural state-law requirements that significantly alter eligibility, computation, and monetization.
1. Mandatory Federal Credit Prerequisite and Industry-Specific "Business Enterprise" Gatekeeping

First, under O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12(b), Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 560-7-8-.42(3), and Georgia Form IT-RD, a business enterprise is eligible for the Georgia Research Tax Credit in a taxable year only if, for the same taxable year, the business enterprise claims and is allowed a federal research credit under Section 41 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended, and attaches a copy of federal Form 6765 to its Georgia income tax return alongside Form IT-RD.

Second, whereas the federal Section 41 credit is available across all industries, O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12(a)(2), Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 560-7-8-.42(2)(b), and Georgia DoR guidance restrict the state credit exclusively to a "business enterprise" (or the headquarters of any such business) engaged in seven statutorily enumerated industries:

items: Manufacturing
Warehousing and distribution
Processing
Telecommunications
Broadcasting
Tourism
Research and development industries.

body.text: Retail businesses are statutorily excluded from the definition of a "business enterprise," though O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12(a)(2) specifies that a business (or its headquarters) that otherwise meets the definition of a business enterprise shall not be considered a retail business merely due to the retail activities of any of its affiliate entities (as defined in O.C.G.A. § 48-7-42(a)).
2. Absolute In-State Geographic Nexus

Under federal law (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(F)), QREs must be conducted within the United States, the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or any possession of the United States. Under O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12(a)(4) and Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 560-7-8-.42(2)(c), Georgia imposes an absolute state-border nexus: "Qualified research expenses" means QREs for any business enterprise as defined in IRC § 41, "except that all wages paid and all purchases of services and supplies must be for research conducted within the State of Georgia". Consequently, W-2 wages paid to remote employees performing research outside Georgia and payments to third-party contractors performing research outside Georgia must be excluded from the Georgia Form IT-RD computation, even if paid from a Georgia corporate headquarters.
3. The 10% Credit Rate and Georgia Gross Receipts Base Amount Formula

Unlike the federal regime—which permits taxpayers to bypass gross receipts by electing the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) under 26 U.S.C. § 41(c)(4)—O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12(a)(1), O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12(c), Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 560-7-8-.42(2)(a), (4), and Form IT-RD mandate a single incremental calculation tied to Georgia gross receipts. Under Rule 560-7-8-.42(2)(a) and Form IT-RD, "Georgia gross receipts" is defined as the numerator of the gross receipts apportionment factor provided in O.C.G.A. § 48-7-31(d).

As set forth on Form IT-RD 2025 (revised 06/20/25) and Rule 560-7-8-.42(2)(a), (4), the credit equals 10 percent of the excess of current-year Georgia QREs over the Base Amount, calculated in three sequential steps:

items: Average Research Ratio (Section 2 & Section 3, Line F): For each of the three preceding taxable years, divide Georgia QREs (Column B) by Georgia Gross Receipts (Column C) to obtain each year's ratio (Column D), sum the three ratios (Line E), and divide by 3 to determine the Average Research Ratio (Line F).
Base Amount (Section 4, Line G): Multiply Current-Year Georgia Gross Receipts by the lesser of the Average Research Ratio (Line F) or 0.300 (the 30 percent statutory cap).

Georgia Research Tax Credit (Section 5, Line H & Line I): Subtract the Base Amount (Line G) from Current-Year Georgia QREs to determine Excess Research Expenses (Line H), and multiply Line H by 0.10 (10 percent) to arrive at the Current-Year Tax Credit (Line I).

body.text: Crucially, under Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 560-7-8-.42(2)(a) and Form IT-RD Section 4, if a business enterprise had no Georgia gross receipts during any one or more of the three preceding taxable years in Column (C) of Section 2, the enterprise cannot use a three-year average ratio; instead, the Base Amount in Line G of Section 4 must be calculated by multiplying current-year Georgia gross receipts by the statutory maximum multiplier of 0.300 (30 percent).
4. The 50% Net Income Tax Cap and Form IT-WH Payroll Withholding Offset

Under O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12(c)–(d), Ga. Comp. R. & Regs. r. 560-7-8-.42(4), and Form IT-RD Section 6, the Georgia Research Tax Credit claimed against income tax in any one taxable year shall not exceed 50 percent of the business enterprise's remaining Georgia net income tax liability after all other tax credits have been applied. In the case of an S corporation or other pass-through entity, Form IT-RD instructs that the allowable credit on Line 7 is first applied to any income tax liability at the entity level and then apportioned to shareholders or partners.

Furthermore, O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12(d) expressly provides that credits applied against quarterly or monthly withholding payments under O.C.G.A. § 48-7-103 and credits against income tax liability under O.C.G.A. § 48-7-20 shall not constitute taxable income to the taxpayer.

To execute the payroll withholding offset, the Georgia DoR mandates that the taxpayer file Form IT-WH (Electronic Notice of Intent) electronically through the Georgia Tax Center (GTC) (electronic filing has been mandatory for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2017, and paper filings are not accepted). The taxpayer's withholding account must be in full compliance with no missing returns or outstanding liabilities. Form IT-WH must be submitted within 30 days of filing the timely original Georgia income tax return (Form 600 or Form 600S) on which the credit (Form IT-RD) is claimed—missing this 30-day window forfeits the payroll withholding benefit for that year. Upon receipt, the Georgia DoR has up to 120 days to review and certify the claim, after which it issues a Letter of Eligibility authorizing the credit to be applied against future withholding payments (the DoR does not refund previous withholding remittances).
5. Impact of Georgia House Bill 1181 (Act No. 598): Carryforward Period Cut from 10 Years to 5 Years

Historically, unused Georgia Research Tax Credits could be carried forward for 10 years from the close of the taxable year in which the qualified research expenses were incurred. On May 6, 2024, Governor Brian Kemp signed House Bill 1181 (Act No. 598, Ga. L. 2024, p. 794, § 1-23), which took effect on January 1, 2025.

Under O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12 as amended by HB 1181, and as confirmed by the Georgia Department of Revenue and Form IT-RD 2025, the statutory carryforward period is bifurcated by tax year vintage. For taxable years beginning before January 1, 2025, unused Georgia Research Tax Credits retain their original 10-year carryforward period. For taxable years beginning on or after January 1, 2025, unused Georgia Research Tax Credits may be carried forward for 5 years (and remain subject in each carryforward year to the 50% cap on remaining Georgia net income tax liability after all other credits). By halving the carryforward horizon from 10 years to 5 years for post-2024 tax years, HB 1181 substantially increases the risk that unused income tax credits will expire unutilized, making immediate monetization via the Form IT-WH payroll withholding election essential for capital-intensive or loss-making enterprises.
Part IV: Judicial Interpretations and Precedential Case Law Governing QREs

Because O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12(a)(4) incorporates 26 U.S.C. § 41 by reference, federal judicial decisions from the U.S. Tax Court, the U.S. Court of Federal Claims, and the U.S. Courts of Appeals—alongside state tax tribunal rulings interpreting IRC § 41—provide the controlling interpretive framework for substantiating QREs.
1. In-House Executive Wages, Substantiation, and IRC § 174(e) Reasonable Compensation: Suder v. Commissioner

In Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201 (decided October 1, 2014), the U.S. Tax Court (Judge Vasquez) issued a foundational opinion addressing (1) whether systematic product development qualified under the Four-Part Test of IRC § 41(d), (2) how in-house wage QREs may be substantiated in the absence of contemporaneous timecards, (3) whether C-suite executives perform qualified services under IRC § 41(b)(2)(B), and (4) as an issue of first impression, how the reasonable compensation limitation of IRC § 174(e) restricts executive wage QREs.

Eric Suder founded Estech Systems, Inc. (ESI) in 1987 out of his garage after purchasing surplus Candela private branch exchanges (PBXs) from Radio Shack for cents on the dollar, growing ESI by 2004 into an ISO-9000-certified designer and manufacturer of proprietary business telephone hardware and software with roughly 125 employees (including ~40 engineers) and $38.5 million in annual gross revenues. During the tax years at issue (2004 through 2007), ESI was an S corporation owned 90% by Mr. Suder (CEO) and 10% by Douglas Boyd (President and COO). ESI claimed research credits across 76 projects (from which the parties stipulated 12 representative sample projects: Arcadia, Chameleon, Clark Kent, Rio Grande, Mad Max, Express FSII, Suzuki, Phoenix, Pony, DLC0, DLC82, and IVC1212), with wages comprising 95% of claimed QREs and supplies comprising 5%. Mr. Suder claimed flow-through research tax credits on his Forms 1040 of $445,987 (2004), $440,306 (2005), $454,526 (2006), and $442,557 (2007), while Mr. Boyd claimed $46,748 (2004), $46,624 (2005), $48,870 (2006), and $48,378 (2007), all of which the IRS disallowed in notices of deficiency along with asserting 20% accuracy-related penalties under IRC § 6662(a).

In fact, the Tax Court record establishes that while an outside consulting firm (alliantgroup) had conducted a study for earlier years (1999–2002), for the 2004–2007 tax years at issue, it was Harvey Wende, ESI's Senior Vice President of Product Operations (2004–2006) and Senior Vice President of Product Development (2007), who personally calculated the percentage of time each employee spent performing qualified services (submitted as Exhibit 445-P), modeling his calculation spreadsheets on the earlier framework. Mr. Wende allocated 75% of CEO Eric Suder's time (conservatively set at 75% to avoid triggering the 80% "substantially all" rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2)), 25% of COO Douglas Boyd's time, and 100% of his own time (Senior VP of Product Development), CTO Buzz Hansen's time, and most engineers', product managers', and product testers' time (while assigning lower percentages to employees who performed routine maintenance work more than sporadically).

The Tax Court opinion confirms that ESI actually paid Mr. Suder a base salary and cash bonuses based on ESI's growth, overall value, and cash flow—totaling $8,674,815 in 2004, $10,954,175 in 2005, $10,548,022 in 2006, and $10,502,584 in 2007 (roughly two-thirds of ESI's total claimed wage QREs). The "patent royalties" were not actual royalty payments from ESI to Mr. Suder; rather, Mr. Suder's compensation expert witness (Mr. Longnecker) constructed a four-part 90th-percentile market compensation benchmark comprising Base Salary, Annual Incentive, Long-Term Incentive, and a hypothetical "Royalties" component ($8,669,645 to $10,170,891 per year, calculated by multiplying ESI's gross revenues by a 22.50% royalty rate to reflect that Mr. Suder was named as an inventor on 13 patents and 1 reissued patent) in an effort to justify Mr. Suder's 8.67M–10.95M annual compensation.
Key Judicial Holdings in Suder v. Commissioner
The Tax Court's holdings in Suder establish four major precedents for corporate and pass-through taxpayers claiming wage and supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(1):

items: Qualification of Systematic Product Development (11 of 12 Representative Projects): Rejecting the IRS's contention that ESI merely selected design alternatives by committee or routine engineering know-how, the Tax Court held that 11 of ESI's 12 representative hardware and software projects satisfied all four tests of IRC § 41(d) (including Clark Kent and Pony, which followed ESI's ISO-9000 development process before being abandoned midway through development, while disallowing one project that involved routine bug-fixing on an already commercially available product). The Court emphasized that ESI followed a structured, multi-level development process influenced by its ISO-9000 certification—beginning with senior product strategy meetings and architectural block diagrams and continuing through alpha and beta testing until all design uncertainties were eliminated.

Substantiation of Wage QREs Without Contemporaneous Timecards: Distinguishing Shami v. Commissioner, 741 F.3d 560 (5th Cir. 2014) (where executives without technical backgrounds offered vague, uncorroborated self-serving testimony), Judge Vasquez held that a taxpayer is not required to maintain contemporaneous hour-by-hour time logs if it provides credible, detailed testimony corroborated by extensive contemporaneous technical documentation (such as ESI's architectural diagrams, engineering schedules, and 170,000+ pages of trial exhibits) establishing that the employees performed qualified services and providing a reliable basis for the percentage allocations under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(1) and Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930).

C-Suite Executives Performing Qualified Services: The Court rejected the IRS's argument that C-suite officers perform solely non-qualifying G&A functions. Because Mr. Suder served as ESI's "chief idea guy" and "product visionary"—spending the vast majority of his time at ESI brainstorming product concepts, researching hardware components, participating in weekly senior product strategy meetings, reviewing schematics, and personally testing every prototype during alpha testing—the Court upheld the 75% allocation for CEO Eric Suder, alongside 25% for COO Douglas Boyd and 100% for CTO Buzz Hansen and Senior VP Harvey Wende.

The IRC § 174(e) Reasonable Compensation Cap: Addressing an issue of first impression under factors articulated in Mayson Manufacturing Co. v. Commissioner and Owensby & Kritikos, Inc. v. Commissioner, the Court held that under 26 U.S.C. § 174(e), wage QREs are allowable only to the extent the compensation is reasonable in amount. Evaluating competing expert reports from Dr. Hafiz (the IRS expert, who proposed upper-quartile limits of $1,046,153 for 2004, $1,018,185 for 2005, $1,078,203 for 2006, and $1,131,436 for 2007) and Mr. Longnecker (petitioners' expert), the Court accepted Mr. Longnecker's 90th-percentile market figures for Base Salary, Annual Incentive, and Long-Term Incentive, but excluded the hypothetical patent royalty component on two grounds: Mr. Suder was never compensated through royalty payments, and royalties are passive payments for the use of intangible property rather than compensation for personal services rendered by an employee. The Court fixed Mr. Suder's total reasonable compensation under IRC § 174(e) at $2,366,090 (2004), $2,439,174 (2005), $2,558,098 (2006), and $2,643,907 (2007)—representing 22.3% to 27.3% of his claimed wages—resulting in net allowable CEO wage QREs (at the 75% qualified service allocation) of $1,774,568 (2004), $1,829,381 (2005), $1,918,574 (2006), and $1,982,930 (2007), while abating all IRC § 6662(a) accuracy-related penalties based on reasonable cause and good faith under IRC § 6664(c)(1) and 26 CFR § 1.6664-4(b).

body.text: 2. The "Mirror-Image" Rules of Contract Research (26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2)) vs. The Funded Research Exclusion (26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) & 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d))

When the taxpayer is the customer/payer claiming 65% contract research expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(3) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2), the customer paying an outside contractor can claim 65% of the payment as a contract research QRE only if the customer bears the financial risk of failure—meaning the contract requires the customer to pay for the research even if the research is not successful (such as a cost-plus, time-and-materials, or unconditional flat-fee research service contract). If payment under a fixed-price contract is contingent on the contractor successfully delivering a working prototype or meeting technical specifications, 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii) treats the customer's payment as the purchase of a "product or result" rather than contract research, disqualifying the customer/payer from claiming a contract research expense.

Conversely, when the taxpayer is the contractor/researcher performing research for a client under 26 U.S.C. § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d) (incorporated via 26 CFR § 1.41-4(c)(9)), the statute excludes from qualified research any activity "to the extent funded by any grant, contract, or otherwise by another person (or governmental entity)". Under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(1)–(2) (formerly § 1.41-5(d)), a performing contractor (such as Fairchild Industries, Lockheed Martin, Dynetics, or Populous Holdings claiming its own in-house engineering wages and supplies) avoids the funded research exclusion only if it satisfies a conjunctive two-prong test: (1) payment to the contractor is contingent on the success of the research (the contractor bears the financial risk of research failure, as is typical in fixed-price deliverable contracts), and (2) the contractor retains "substantial rights" in the research results. Notably, if payment is contingent on success (barring the customer/payer from claiming contract research expenses under § 1.41-2(e)(2)(iii)) and the researcher retains no substantial rights under § 1.41-4A(d)(2) (barring the researcher from claiming QREs), neither party can claim the research credit.

body.text: Detailed Analysis of the Four Funded-Research Precedents

items: Fairchild Industries, Inc. v. United States, 71 F.3d 868 (Fed. Cir. Nov. 29, 1995; modified Feb. 23, 1996): In July 1982, Fairchild entered into a fixed-price incentive contract with the U.S. Air Force for the Full-Scale Development (FSD) phase of the T-46A Next Generation Trainer aircraft, requiring Fairchild to develop and deliver two prototype aircraft and bear "Total System Responsibility" across more than 1,000 pages of technical specifications. Between 1982 and 1986, Fairchild spent $216,056,000 against an amended FSD ceiling price of $133,485,885 (incurring unrecovered research costs exceeding $95 million), ultimately receiving 120.6million(53.0 million in liquidated progress payments, $60.8 million in unliquidated progress payments, and $6.8 million upon settlement) when Congress canceled the program at 90% FSD completion. Out of 109.4millioninreportedFSDresearchexpensesonits1982–1985returns(89.8 million remaining after unrelated disallowances), the IRS disallowed 55.8% ($50.3 million, calculated as the ratio of $120.6M paid by the Air Force to $216.1M total FSD costs), resulting in $5.8 million of disallowed research tax credits for 1983 and 1984 on the ground that the Air Force's bimonthly progress payments "funded" the research under IRC § 44F(d)(3). Reversing the Court of Federal Claims (30 Fed. Cl. 839), the Federal Circuit held that the availability of the credit turns on "who bears the research costs upon failure, not on whether the researcher is likely to succeed in performing the project". Because Defense Acquisition Regulations (DAR 7-302.2 and 7-302.4) entitled the Air Force to reject unsatisfactory work, demand correction at Fairchild's expense, or impose an equitable price reduction—and because all unliquidated progress payments were refundable financing advances if line items were not delivered and accepted—Fairchild bore the financial risk of failure and its QREs were not funded.

Lockheed Martin Corp. v. United States, 210 F.3d 1366 (Fed. Cir. Apr. 26, 2000): Evaluating refund claims for tax years 1982 through 1988 across roughly 300 fixed-price defense contracts through four major representative programs (LANTIRN, SICBM, Titan IV, and SLAT), the Court of Federal Claims (42 Fed. Cl. 485) had ruled that Lockheed Martin (as successor to Martin Marietta) retained no "substantial rights" under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2) (formerly § 1.41-5(d)) because the government held unlimited rights in technical data and software, imposed security classifications and export controls, and required nonrecurring-cost recoupment payments on commercial sales. The Federal Circuit reversed on the substantial rights issue, holding that "[t]he right to use the research results, even without the exclusive right, is a substantial right". Because Lockheed Martin retained the right to use the underlying engineering results in its trade or business without paying a license fee to the government (and granted the government a nonexclusive license to subject inventions), external export controls, security classifications, and commercial sales recoupment clauses did not render the research funded. On a separate procedural issue involving the LANTIRN program, the Federal Circuit affirmed the lower court's ruling under the substantial-variance doctrine barring Lockheed Martin from expanding its refund claims during litigation to include employee-related expenses not previously detailed in the administrative "Green Books" schedules submitted to the IRS.

Dynetics, Inc. & Subsidiaries v. United States, 121 Fed. Cl. 492 (2015): As documented in IRS Field Attorney Advice 20223401F and the Eighth Circuit's decision in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, Inc. v. Commissioner, 100 F.4th 986 (8th Cir. May 6, 2024) (which likewise followed Dynetics and Geosyntec Consultants, Inc. v. United States, 776 F.3d 1330 (11th Cir. 2015) in holding that general professional standards of care and economic risk do not make payment contingent on technical research success), the Dynetics court held that (a) even where a contract includes an inspection clause, payment is not contingent on research success if the contract lacks express rejection language and does not limit payment solely to accepted deliverables (121 Fed. Cl. at 505, 515–16), and (b) where a contract incorporates a DD Form 254 (Department of Defense Contract Security Classification Specification) prohibiting the contractor from using classified intelligence results without express government permission, or a university IP clause vesting all patentable, nonpatentable, and "other intellectual property rights" in the client, the contractor fails the substantial rights test—because general engineering skills and advancements developed during contract performance are merely non-qualifying "incidental benefits" under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(2). Furthermore, under the default stacking rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d)(3), where a contractor retains substantial rights under a partially funded contract, third-party funding stacks first against otherwise creditable QREs (meaning only cost overruns exceeding the client's funding may qualify unless an allocation exception is approved), whereas if the contractor lacks substantial rights under § 1.41-4A(d)(2), even excess cost overruns are barred from QRE eligibility.

Populous Holdings, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Docket No. 405-17 (Order signed Dec. 6, 2019; served Dec. 9, 2019): Applying Fairchild Industries and Lockheed Martin to private-sector architectural and structural engineering, Judge Goeke evaluated five representative fixed-price contracts (McEnery, Houston Dynamo, University of Arkansas (UA), University of South Florida (USF), and Pico Hall) out of more than 100 contracts for tax years 2010 (151,494generalbusinesscreditcarryforward)and2011(132,539 research credit). Granting summary judgment for Populous and denying the IRS's cross-motion, the Tax Court held that (a) under fixed-price contracts where the firm is paid for a final work product (with USF requiring payment upon approval of each phase/deliverable, Houston Dynamo and Pico Hall expressly requiring Populous to revise documents at its own expense, and capped reimbursements in McEnery, Houston Dynamo, and UA limited to non-research items like travel and printing) and must remedy failed design research at its own expense without additional compensation, payment is contingent on research success, and (b) client ownership of physical construction documents, models, renderings, and architectural copyrights in the three contracts challenged on rights (McEnery, Pico Hall, and Houston Dynamo) did not deprive Populous of substantial rights, because Populous retained copies of documents for its own use and nothing in the contracts prohibited Populous from using the underlying technological research know-how in future projects or required it to pay clients for that use.

body.text: 3. The Process of Experimentation and Production Supplies: Union Carbide vs. Appeals of Swat-Fame, Inc.

Even when a taxpayer incurs internal wages and supplies in-house, those expenditures fail to qualify under IRC § 41(b)(1) if the underlying project fails the Process of Experimentation test of IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) or represents routine commercial production costs.

In Union Carbide Corp. & Subsidiaries v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2009-50 (97 T.C.M. (CCH) 1207, decided March 10, 2009), aff'd, 697 F.3d 104 (2d Cir. 2012), the Tax Court and the Second Circuit established two foundational rules governing IRC § 41(d) and § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). First, regarding the scientific method standard for a process of experimentation, the Tax Court held that a valid process of experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) "requires the use of the scientific method," defined as "a methodical plan involving a series of trials to test a hypothesis, analyze the data, refine the hypothesis, and retest the hypothesis so that it constitutes experimentation in the scientific sense". For example, Union Carbide's "anticoking project" (aimed at reducing carbon buildup in chemical furnaces) satisfied the 80% process of experimentation threshold because the company systematically collected and analyzed data comparing existing technologies against experimental alternatives, whereas another project failed because Union Carbide did not conduct post-test analysis. Second, regarding the disallowance of raw materials and wages used in ordinary commercial production, while affirming that the development or improvement of a manufacturing process is evaluated as a separate business component from the product itself under IRC § 41(d)(2)(C) even after the underlying product is in commercial production, the Tax Court and the Second Circuit (697 F.3d 104) held that the baseline cost of raw materials consumed during plant-scale process trials—materials that Union Carbide would have purchased and used to manufacture commercial product for sale regardless of whether process research was occurring—cannot be claimed as supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii), nor do production employee wages that would have been incurred regardless of research qualify under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i); only additional, incremental costs specifically attributable to evaluating the experimental process qualify.

Conversely, in Appeals of Swat-Fame, Inc., et al., 2020-OTA-046P (California Office of Tax Appeals, Opinion issued March 22, 2019; Case Nos. 18010702, 18012114, & 18012115), an S corporation women's and girls' apparel designer creating roughly 600 styles per month and its shareholders (Bruce & Judith Stern and Mitchell & Nina Quaranta) claimed R&D tax credit refunds for fiscal/tax years 2008–2011 and contested Franchise Tax Board (FTB) proposed assessments for 2012 totaling $2,443,508 under IRC § 41 and California Revenue & Taxation Code § 23609. Specifically, the disputed amounts comprised 607,474attheSwat-Fameentitylevel(26,143 for 2008, $51,168 for 2009, $107,728 for 2010, $75,008 for 2011, and $347,427 for 2012), 1,008,164fortheSterns(158,754 for 2008, $143,530 for 2009, $196,952 for 2010, $165,883 for 2011, and $343,045 for 2012), and 827,870fortheQuarantas(107,635 for 2008, $102,129 for 2009, $117,759 for 2010, $169,999 for 2011, and $330,348 for 2012). The parties stipulated to resolve the entire dispute based on four sample garment projects: (1) Project UB636N (2008 indigo stretch denim Bermuda shorts made of 98% cotton and 2% spandex experiencing waistband shrinkage during lasering/washing and tearing back pockets), (2) Project D11072 (2009 party slip dress with adjustable thin "spaghetti" straps supporting heavy jacquard fabric and a flat charmeuse cummerbund), (3) Project Z1743D01 (2010 two-piece ruffle skirt and leggings set addressing ruffle counts per size and splitting legging seams), and (4) Project M93771 (2010 two-piece cotton sundress with a flat-lying smocked band and cropped shrug).

While the OTA noted factually that Swat-Fame employed no chemists and did not send fabrics to outside vendors for chemical testing, the Panel explicitly declined to rule on the Technological in Nature test, the Section 174 test, or the Business Component test, stating verbatim: "we need not discuss the other tests for qualified research (i.e., the Section 174 test, the technological information test, and the business component test)" because Swat-Fame failed the Process of Experimentation test under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) and § 41(d)(3)(B) on all four sample projects. Specifically, the OTA held that resolving ripped pocket corners caused by stonewashing by adding extra bar tack stitching, or preventing seam splitting on leggings by switching from a five-thread overlock stitch to a four-thread overlock stitch, was the routine application of a known industry solution through simple trial and error rather than a structured scientific process of experimentation (such as recording wash temperatures, testing hypotheses, and re-testing under identical conditions). Furthermore, under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4(a)(5)(ii), activities driven by style, taste, cosmetic, or seasonal design factors (such as denim lasering/washing for visual appearance or fitting garments to customer aesthetic preferences) do not constitute a qualified purpose. Because Swat-Fame failed to demonstrate that at least 80 percent ("substantially all") of its activities for any of the four sample projects constituted elements of a process of experimentation for a qualified purpose (and failed to substantiate subcomponents for the shrinking-back rule of 26 CFR § 1.41-4(b)(2)), it engaged in no qualified research and generated zero QREs.
Part V: IRS Specificity Requirements for Refund Claims and IRC § 280C Coordination
1. Evolution of the IRS Refund Claim Specificity Mandate: From Five Elements (2021) to Three Elements (June 18, 2024–2026)

On October 15, 2021, the IRS issued Information Release IR-2021-203 accompanying Office of Chief Counsel Field Attorney Advice Memorandum 20214101F, establishing strict procedural specificity requirements under 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1) for any administrative claim for refund or credit on an amended return (or Administrative Adjustment Request) involving the IRC § 41 research credit filed on or after January 10, 2022.

Under Memorandum 20214101F, a taxpayer filing a Section 41 refund claim was initially required to provide five items of information verified by a written declaration signed under penalties of perjury at the time of filing:

items: Identify all the business components (as defined in IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)) to which the Section 41 research credit claim relates for that claim year;
For each business component, identify all research activities performed;

Identify (by name or, per FAQ 10 updated June 18, 2024, by listing the specific number of individuals and each individual's title or position, which may be aggregated by group per FAQ 11) all individuals who performed each research activity;
Identify all the information each individual sought to discover; and
Provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year (which may be reported via Form 6765).

body.text: First, effective for all Section 41 refund claims postmarked on or after June 18, 2024, the IRS waived the requirement to include Item 3 (the names/positions of the individuals who performed each research activity) and Item 4 (the information each individual sought to discover) at the time the refund claim is initially filed, though the IRS reserves the right to request Items 3 and 4 if the claim is selected for substantive examination. Thus, for refund claims postmarked on or after June 18, 2024, taxpayers must provide three mandatory items at filing (plus a signed declaration under penalties of perjury): (1) identify all business components forming the factual basis of the claim under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B), (2) describe all research activities performed by business component (specifying what the taxpayer did and how they did it, rather than merely restating Code or regulatory language), and (3) provide total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses (which may be satisfied by properly completing Form 6765). Additionally, under FAQ 13, Partnerships subject to the Bipartisan Budget Act (BBA) must submit an Administrative Adjustment Request (AAR) attaching the required items alongside Forms 8985/8986, whereas non-BBA pass-through entities (such as S corporations) must attach the required specificity items both to the entity's amended return and to the partners' or shareholders' amended returns alongside their amended Schedules K-1. Under FAQ 17, Form 1120 corporate taxpayers cannot file an informal refund claim for the Research Credit and must file a formal amended return pursuant to Notice 2008-39, and under FAQ 18, taxpayers utilizing statistical sampling under Rev. Proc. 2011-42 must provide the required specificity items for all sample units attached to the claim.

Second, if the IRS determines that a timely filed refund claim is procedurally deficient, it issues Letter 6426C or Letter 6428 (Claim for Credit for Increasing Research Credit Activities - Additional Information Required) notifying the taxpayer of the missing items and granting 45 days from the letter's issue date to perfect the claim (submitted via paper or facsimile only, accompanied by a signed declaration under penalties of perjury; portable electronic storage devices are rejected). While LB&I-04-0125-0001 initially extended this 45-day perfection transition period through January 10, 2026, the IRS subsequently extended the transition period a second time through January 10, 2027. In both the initial filing and any 45-day perfection response, Memorandum 20214101F strictly prohibits a "data dump" of voluminous unindexed technical records; if the taxpayer relies on supporting documents or a credit study, it must specify the exact page(s) where the required facts appear. If a taxpayer fails to perfect a deficient claim within the 45-day window (and after mandatory concurrence from both management—the Territory Manager for LB&I or Planning and Special Programs (PSP) Section Chief for SB/SE—and IRS Division Counsel), the IRS issues Letter 6430 (No Consideration, Section 41 Claim) and inputs a Form 3870 / TC 290 for zero to release the master file freeze code, rejecting the claim procedurally without reaching its merits or issuing a formal notice of claim disallowance. Because a procedurally rejected claim is not considered for any purpose as a duly filed refund claim under 26 CFR § 301.6402-2(b)(1), the taxpayer has failed to exhaust administrative remedies under 26 U.S.C. § 7422(a), depriving federal courts of subject-matter jurisdiction over a subsequent refund suit if the IRC § 6511(a) statute of limitations has expired. In parallel with its refund claim rules, the IRS revised Form 6765 to add Section E (Other Information), Section F (Qualified Research Expenses Summary), and Section G (Business Component Information); under the IRS Instructions for Form 6765 (revised through June 28, 2026), completing Section G is optional for tax years beginning before 2026 (including the 2025 tax year) and mandatory for tax years beginning after 2025 (including the 2026 tax year), unless the filer is a qualified small business under § 41(h)(3) electing the payroll tax credit or has controlled-group QREs of $1.5 million or less and prior three-year average annual gross receipts of $50 million or less under § 448(c)(3) on an original return.
2. Coordination of QRE Credits and Deductions Under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)

To prevent taxpayers from claiming both a full deduction (or capital account amortization) and a full tax credit on the exact same dollar of QREs, 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c) mandates strict coordination between IRC § 41 and IRC § 174 / § 174A. Under the statutory text of 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(1), if the amount of the research credit determined for the taxable year under IRC § 41(a)(1) exceeds the amount allowable as a deduction for such taxable year for qualified research expenses or basic research expenses, the amount chargeable to capital account for the taxable year for such expenses must be reduced by the amount of such excess; and under IRM 8.7.1.4.1 and the IRS ATG, where QREs are otherwise deductible, no deduction is allowed for that portion of the QREs equal to the full research credit determined under § 41(a) unless a reduced credit election is made. Alternatively, under 26 U.S.C. § 280C(c)(2) (formerly codified at § 280C(c)(3)), a taxpayer may avoid the § 280C(c)(1) reduction by electing a reduced research credit—calculated under § 280C(c)(2)(B) as the excess of (i) the gross credit determined under § 41(a) without regard to § 280C(c)(2), over (ii) the product of that credit and the maximum corporate tax rate under 26 U.S.C. § 11(b) (currently 21%, yielding a net reduced regular credit rate of 15.8% or a net reduced ASC rate of 11.06%, compared to the historical 13% reduced regular credit rate under the pre-2018 35% corporate tax rate noted in the ATG). Under IRC § 280C(c)(2)(C), IRM 8.7.1.4.1, and the IRS ATG, this election must be made annually on Form 6765 on an original timely filed tax return (including extensions) by actually computing and claiming the reduced credit, is irrevocable once made, and cannot be made on an amended return or via a "protective" statement merely writing "280C" on an original return.
Part VI: Applied Scenarios: QRE Qualification and Monetization in Georgia
The following three hypothetical scenarios illustrate how QRE rules operate across Georgia's core industrial sectors.
Scenario 1 (Hypothetical): Warehousing and Distribution Innovation in Atlanta

Taxpayer & Industry Eligibility: "Peach State Logistics Hub, LLC" (PSLH) is a hypothetical third-party logistics (3PL) firm headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia, operating under NAICS Code 493 (Warehousing and Storage), which qualifies as an eligible "business enterprise" under O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12(a)(2) ("warehousing and distribution"). PSLH undertakes an engineering project to develop a proprietary AI-driven Warehouse Management System (WMS) integrated with experimental Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) capable of routing non-standard pallet geometries. The project satisfies the Four-Part Test of IRC § 41(d)(1) because the spatial-mapping neural network architecture is uncertain at the outset (§ 174 / § 174A test), relies on computer science and robotics engineering (Technological in Nature), targets a new software and hardware business component (Business Component test), and evaluates multiple routing algorithms through simulation and live collision trials (Process of Experimentation).

Segregating Federal and Georgia QREs Under IRC § 41(b)(1) and O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12(a)(4): For in-house wages under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i), PSLH captures W-2 wages (IRC § 3401(a)) paid to software engineers coding the WMS algorithm (actual conduct) and warehouse technicians operating the AGVs during live experimental trials (direct support), strictly limited to personnel physically performing their work in Atlanta, Georgia. For in-house supplies under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii) and (C), non-depreciable tangible raw materials and lidar sensors used to construct experimental AGV pilot models during collision testing qualify as supply QREs under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4), whereas the depreciable server hardware hosting the WMS is excluded under IRC § 41(b)(2)(C)(ii). For contract research under IRC § 41(b)(3)(A) and 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2), PSLH engages an external robotics laboratory at Georgia Tech in Atlanta to perform qualified research on a weight-distribution sensor array.

Recomputed Step-by-Step Georgia Credit and Form IT-WH Calculation: Assume PSLH reports $50,000,000 in current-year Georgia gross receipts, $2,500,000 in current-year Georgia QREs, a preceding three-year average Georgia QRE-to-gross-receipts ratio of 3.5% (0.035), and $20,000 in remaining Georgia corporate net income tax liability after all other credits. Applying the statutory formula of O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12 and Form IT-RD 2025, PSLH's Base Amount is 1,750,000(50,000,000 × 0.035), yielding 750,000inexcessQREs(2,500,000 minus $1,750,000) and a 10% Georgia Research Tax Credit of $75,000. Because the 50% income tax cap limits PSLH's income tax offset to $10,000 (50% of $20,000), PSLH files Form IT-WH electronically via the Georgia Tax Center within 30 days of filing its original return to apply the remaining $65,000 directly against its Georgia payroll withholding obligations.
