body.text: Scenario 2 (Hypothetical): Aerospace Defense Contracting in Warner Robins, Georgia

In a second hypothetical scenario, an aerospace engineering contractor operating in Warner Robins, Georgia, designs high-energy Electronic Warfare (EW) jamming pods for the U.S. Department of Defense. Resolving severe thermal dissipation uncertainties requires iterative structural and aerodynamic modeling alongside destructive wind-tunnel testing of composite prototype housings. Because the contractor performs this work under a fixed-price contract that conditions payment on the pods passing rigorous military acceptance testing (placing the financial risk of failed research on the contractor under Fairchild Industries, 71 F.3d 868) and permits the contractor to use the underlying thermal management know-how in future commercial avionics projects without paying a license fee to the government (retaining substantial rights under Lockheed Martin, 210 F.3d 1366, and Populous Holdings, Docket No. 405-17)—and avoids the disqualifying DD Form 254 intelligence prohibitions or university IP assignments that defeated the claim in Dynetics, 121 Fed. Cl. 492, as well as the absence of rejection clauses that defeated the claim in Meyer, Borgman & Johnson, 100 F.4th 986—the contractor's research is unfunded under IRC § 41(d)(4)(H) and 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d). Consequently, the W-2 wages of its Georgia-based aerospace engineers and the non-depreciable composite materials used to build the wind-tunnel test models qualify as in-house QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2) and O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12(a)(4), and excess state credits can be monetized against payroll withholding via Form IT-WH.
Scenario 3 (Hypothetical): Biotechnology and Living "Pilot Models" Under George v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2026-10)

In George v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2026-10 (Feb. 3, 2026), Judge Greaves evaluated amended 2012–2014 tax returns claiming $4.47 million in research tax credits filed by shareholders of George's of Missouri, Inc. (GOMI), an S corporation operating the live-production side of a vertically integrated poultry producer that engaged alliantgroup in 2014 to conduct a retroactive R&D study across seven research trial categories. The Tax Court established three major holdings directly governing supply QREs and credit computations under IRC § 41(b)(1):

items: Living Subjects and Feed as Qualifying "Pilot Model" Supply QREs: Rejecting the IRS's argument that raising experimental flocks of broiler chickens constituted ordinary commercial production and that prior vendor lab testing eliminated uncertainty, the Court applied the 2014 pilot-model regulations (26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4)) and held that because real-world farm variables (fluctuating temperatures, environmental conditions, and biological interactions) created taxpayer-specific uncertainty regarding performance under GOMI's operating conditions, physical test flocks raised to evaluate and resolve uncertainty regarding an improved product (healthier, more uniform broilers) function as pilot models, and the feed costs incurred to raise them qualify as supply QREs under IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii). Furthermore, the Court held that GOMI's decision not to claim any employee wage QREs (because management concluded calculating wage allocations was not worth the effort) did not preclude GOMI from claiming supply QREs.

Contemporaneous Production Logs Outweigh Retroactive Study Narratives: Across all evaluated projects, GOMI substantiated $14,315,418 in total QREs (22.7% of the amount originally claimed, with 77.3% disallowed), including $7,280,578 for 2013 probiotic gut-health trials (Sporulin and Calsporin, where GOMI hypothesized efficacy, tested, analyzed data, and iterated upon failure), $1,521,039 for a 2014 laryngotracheitis (LT) vector-vaccine priming trial, $398,520 for a 2014 Ross 708 vs. Cobb 500 genetic line trial (which the Court praised as the "cleanest example of the scientific method" due to its control group and slaughter-margin data analysis), and its 2012 HatchPak and Tylan trial. However, the Court allowed $0 for trials where GOMI's contemporaneous daily feed recipes and barn logs contradicted the retroactive study—including Salinomycin and Phytase enzyme trials (~$1.2 million in QREs at risk, where feed logs showed a constant 0.4 lbs/ton dosage rather than experimental variations), Floramax probiotics (~$680,000 in QREs at risk, where no records tracked which flocks received the additive), 2013 HatchPak/Tylan (~$2.87 million credit year partially disallowed because scientific uncertainty had already been resolved in 2012), and 2012–2013 LT vaccine delivery and Vaxxitek IBD trials (where witnesses could not establish whether trials occurred in 2012 or 2013 or set aside control flocks).

Rejection of the Cohan Rule for Base-Period QREs and Reduction of ASC Rate from 14% to 6%: Although GOMI elected the 14% Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC), it failed to substantiate its QREs for the three preceding base years (2009–2011), instead attempting to estimate base-year QREs by applying a 10.23% ratio derived from the credit years. Declaring that the Court "will not wing it with an estimate ungrounded in the record," Judge Greaves refused to apply the Cohan rule and reduced GOMI's allowable ASC credit rate from 14 percent down to 6 percent of substantiated current-year QREs pursuant to IRC § 41(c)(5)(B) [now § 41(c)(4)(B)] (while abating IRC § 6662 accuracy-related penalties due to good-faith reliance on a comprehensive professional study).

body.text: Part VIII: Strategic Synthesis for Section 41(b)(1) QRE Compliance

For corporate and pass-through taxpayers operating in the State of Georgia as of 2026, capturing and defending Qualified Research Expenses under 26 U.S.C. § 41(b)(1) and O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12 requires rigorous adherence to five operational rules:

items: Strict Segregation of Section 41(b)(1) Cost Categories: Claimants must isolate W-2 wages under IRC § 3401(a) (applying the 80% "substantially all" safe harbor of 26 CFR § 1.41-2(d)(2) only where substantiated by employee-level records, evaluating stock options by grant-year duties and exercise-year spreads, and capping executive compensation at market reasonableness under IRC § 174(e) per Suder v. Commissioner), non-depreciable tangible supplies and pilot models under 26 CFR § 1.174-2(a)(4) (excluding routine production raw materials per Union Carbide and indirect overhead on self-constructed supplies per the IRS CIP), and qualifying off-premises computer time-sharing under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(b)(4).

Contractual Alignment with the "Mirror-Image" Risk Rules: Before claiming 65% contract research expenses as a payer under 26 CFR § 1.41-2(e)(2), the taxpayer must verify that the prior agreement obligates the payer to bear the cost even if the research fails; conversely, when performing contracted engineering or development for clients, the taxpayer must ensure that payment is contingent on technical success (backed by express rejection/remedy clauses) and that it retains non-exclusive rights to use the underlying research know-how under 26 CFR § 1.41-4A(d) (Fairchild Industries, Lockheed Martin, Populous Holdings, Dynetics, and Meyer, Borgman & Johnson).

Contemporaneous Business-Component Substantiation: As demonstrated in George v. Commissioner (T.C. Memo. 2026-10) and Appeals of Swat-Fame, Inc. (2020-OTA-046P)—and reinforced by mandatory Section G reporting on Form 6765 for tax years beginning after 2025—taxpayers must maintain contemporaneous operational logs (both for current credit years and historical base years) linking each business component to a systematic scientific process of experimentation.

Compliance with Updated IRS Refund Specificity Rules: When claiming Section 41 credits on amended returns postmarked on or after June 18, 2024, taxpayers must include the three mandatory items under updated IRS guidance (LB&I-04-0125-0001 and Amended Return FAQs)—identifying all business components, describing all research activities performed by business component, and reporting total wage, supply, and contract QREs—to avoid procedural rejection under Letter 6430.

Georgia Nexus Isolation and Immediate Form IT-WH Monetization: Finally, eligible Georgia business enterprises must strip out all out-of-state wages, supplies, and contractor costs under O.C.G.A. § 48-7-40.12(a)(4), compute their Base Amount using the lesser of their three-year Georgia QRE-to-gross-receipts ratio or 0.300 on Form IT-RD, and—where credits exceed the 50% net income tax cap—file Form IT-WH electronically via the Georgia Tax Center within 30 days of their original return to convert excess credits into immediate payroll withholding cash flow rather than risking expiration under HB 1181's five-year carryforward limit.
